message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

The case for Sunday opening is well supported. The case for evening opening is overstated, though, and the costings contain an addition error. Several of the strongest claims in the conclusion and in your summary are not borne out by the document's own tables.

## 1. The cost table doesn't add up to £174,000

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Staffing | £124,000 |
| Utilities and caretaking | £32,500 |
| Kiosk maintenance | £7,500 |
| **Actual total** | **£164,000** |

The line items are each correct (10 × 2 × 50 × 5 = 5,000 hours at £24.80 = £124,000, and £6,500 × 5 = £32,500), but the stated total is **£10,000 too high**. Either a line is missing or the bid should be for £164,000. A Finance reviewer will spot this, and it undermines the "carefully costed" framing more than the money itself does.

## 2. Evening use is well below daytime, not "close to" it

| Slot | Visits per hour | As a share of weekday daytime |
|---|---|---|
| Weekday 9–12 | 46 | |
| Weekday 12–5 | 58 | |
| **Tue/Thu 5–8 (new)** | **21** | **about 36–46%** |
| Sunday 11–3 (new) | 52 | about 90–113% |

The document says evening visits "averaged close to the weekday daytime level" in Section 3 and repeats it in the conclusion. Your summary repeats it too. **Evening use is less than half of daytime use.** Sunday is the slot that comes close to daytime levels.

This doesn't make evenings worthless. The job club filling up is real evidence of value, but the claim needs correcting. The paper should also say plainly that the evening hours cost the same as the Sunday hours per hour but attract about 40% of the visits.

## 3. The pilot lasted six months, not twelve

Section 3 gives October 2025 to March 2026, which is six months. The conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." It also ran entirely through **autumn and winter**, which matters in two ways:
- **Evening visits** in dark winter months may not represent summer evenings. They could be higher or lower.
- **Utilities were "scaled to a full year"** from winter spending, when heating and lighting peak. The utilities line is probably *overstated*, which errs on the prudent side, but the paper should say so.

## 4. The visit forecast assumes every branch matches Ashgrove

The 84,000 figure is correct arithmetic on Ashgrove's rates: (6 h × 21 + 4 h × 52) × 50 weeks × 5 branches ≈ 83,500. But:
- **Ashgrove is the busiest branch.** Section 7 says the other four "may be lower," yet Section 5 applies Ashgrove's rates to all five.
- **Some visits will be displaced, not additional.** People who shift a Saturday or weekday visit to Sunday add no new use.
- **Cost per visit compares a marginal cost with an average one.** At £164,000 / 84,000, the figure is about £1.95. The £3.40 borough average includes buildings, stock and management, so the two figures don't measure the same thing. The comparison flatters the bid.

Showing a range, for example with the other branches at 60–80% of Ashgrove's rate, would be more credible.

## 5. The membership increase isn't attributed to the new hours

New memberships rose from 690 to 1,140, which is +65%, so "about two-thirds" is accurate. But these are **branch-wide** figures for the period, not sign-ups made during the new hours. Without that breakdown, or a comparison with the other branches over the same months, the increase may partly reflect other factors, such as promotion of the pilot itself or wider trends.

## 6. The self-service comparison is incomplete

Your summary says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The document doesn't actually make that calculation. The figures it gives work out as follows:

- **Annual staffing saving:** about £83,000 (two-thirds of £124,000).
- **One-off building works:** £60,000 × 5 = £300,000, which is *capital*, not revenue.
- **Payback on the building works:** about **3.6 years**, after which self-service would be cheaper each year.

The stronger reason in the paper is that unstaffed hours **couldn't support the job club and family activities**, which the pilot suggests drive much of the value. Lead with that, and either present the cost comparison over several years or drop the claim that it costs more. It is also unclear why self-service would keep a third of the staffing cost, and that needs a sentence of explanation.

A smaller query: a **kiosk maintenance contract** sits oddly in a bid built on fully staffed opening. Explain why it's needed.

## 7. What holds up

- **The rationale is clear and tied to evidence.** 44% of working-age non-users say the hours are the barrier, and the bid links this to Council Plan commitments.
- **The staffing calculation is sound and transparent.** The two-person lone-working requirement is explained, and the rate build-up (grade midpoint + 28% on-costs + Sunday enhancement) is stated.
- **Utilities are based on actual pilot spending,** not estimates.
- **Sunday opening is strongly supported** at 52 visits an hour, with clear family use.
- **The job club evidence** is specific and persuasive for the evening slot.
- **The risks section is honest** about the other branches possibly being less busy.

## Notes on the author's summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Evening visits close to daytime levels" | Incorrect: 21 against 46–58 |
| "Sums to £174,000" | Line items sum to £164,000 |
| "Tested the exact opening pattern" | True, but at one branch, the busiest, over six winter months |
| New memberships "up by about two-thirds" | Accurate, but not attributed to the new hours |
| Self-service "would cost more once building works are included" | Not shown; cheaper after about 3.6 years |
| Utilities "from actual pilot spend" | True, though probably overstated because of winter scaling |

## Recommended changes

1. **Fix the total** to £164,000, or add the missing £10,000 line.
2. **Correct the evening claim** in Section 3 and the conclusion. Present evenings and Sundays separately, with their own cost per visit.
3. **Change "twelve-month" to "six-month,"** and note the winter timing.
4. **Give a visit forecast range** for the other four branches, and mention displacement.
5. **Drop the comparison with the £3.40 average**, or compare like with like.
6. **Rework the self-service section** around service value, with a multi-year cost comparison if cost is kept.
7. **Consider an option** of Sunday opening at all five branches, plus evenings where there is evidence such as job club demand. It would cost less and draw on the strongest pilot results.

The bid has good evidence behind it. Correcting these points will make it easier for Members to approve and harder for scrutiny to pick apart.
